headlines.description: An ambitious and self-described “first-of-its-kind system” designed to hold San Francisco politicians accountable for sexual misconduct failed its very first test, leaving a sexual assault complaint unanswered for nearly four months. The NBC Bay Area Investigative Unit uncovered a basic oversight that party leaders say contributed to the failure: the person responsible for reviewing complaints was never told how often to check the inbox. The new reporting system was supposed to fill a gap in political accountability. As NBC Bay Area reported last year, political campaigns – unlike traditional workplaces – often lack formal procedures for reporting and investigating sexual misconduct. San Francisco’s Democratic Party had also been marred by sexual misconduct allegations against several prominent figures in local Democratic politics. In response, the San Francisco Democratic County Central Committee, or DCCC, recruited volunteers from across the country, consulted survivors of sexual abuse, and enlisted pro bono attorneys to research allegations and build a reporting process independent of party leadership. When the first complaint arrived, however, the system failed at its most basic task – ensuring someone responded. “At best, they were neglecting their responsibilities,” said Brad Chapin, a San Francisco-based political organizer who submitted the complaint. “At worst, it was intentional to protect and provide cover for Manny.” Manny Yekutiel, once considered a leading candidate for a seat on San Francisco’s Board of Supervisors, is the politician Chapin accused of sexual assault. Yekutiel did not respond to NBC Bay Area’s request for comment but has publicly denied the allegations. After two other men accused him of sexual misconduct on Oct. 1, Yekutiel dropped out of the race, but continued to deny assaulting anyone. At a house party in 2020, Chapin says Yekutiel cornered him and stuck his hand down Chapin’s pants. “I think I was just sort of shocked,” Chapin said. “Like, what is happening?” In a police report Chapin filed in April, he said Yekutiel grabbed his testicles in an “aggressive manner…like an animal.” “I tried to get away,” Chapin said during an interview with the NBC Bay Area Investigative Unit. “I was like begging him to let me go and he would squeeze harder and pull me back.” Yekutiel has not been charged with a crime, but the San Francisco Police Department told NBC Bay Area the “case remains open.” Text messages Chapin provided to NBC Bay Area show he told a friend about the alleged assault shortly after it happened, but for years Chapin didn’t formally report the incident to law enforcement or officials at the San Francisco Democratic Party. That changed when Chapin learned of Yekutiel’s campaign for San Francisco’s District 8 Supervisor seat, which includes the Castro, Noe Valley, and parts of the Mission District. Chapin worried that, if elected, Yekutiel could use his position of power to harm others, a fear Chapin said was rooted in what he described as Yekutiel’s brazen behavior during the alleged assault. “If he was willing to do that, in that way, within just seconds of seeing me … there’s no way he only did it to me,” Chapin said. “I kind of had the sense that it would be really hard for most people to come forward.” Brad Chapin formally submitted a complaint through the San Francisco Democratic Party’s sexual misconduct reporting system, alleging he was sexually assaulted in 2020 by Manny Yekutiel, a well-known bookstore owner and, at one point, a leading political candidate in the race for District 8 Supervisor in San Francisco. Documents Chapin provided to NBC Bay Area show that he submitted an official complaint to San Francisco’s Democratic Party on March 3, detailing the alleged assault. After more than a month of silence, Chapin submitted his complaint a second time on April 16. A week later, he also reported the assault to the San Francisco Police Department. While police detectives followed up with Chapin as part of their investigation, two more months went by with Chapin still not receiving any response from the judicial arm of San Francisco’s Democratic Party. Chapin then went to the press with his allegations. On June 30, the San Francisco Standard published a story on Chapin’s allegations. Within hours of that story’s publication, San Francisco’s Democratic Party finally responded. The ombudsperson, responsible for receiving complaints under the party’s new reporting system, e-mailed Chapin saying his “complaint has been received and is currently under review.” That message came nearly four months after he initially reported the sexual assault to the San Francisco Democratic Party. “That’s when I heard back from them,” Chapin recalled. “It was hard not to feel that it was to provide cover for Manny.” The Democratic Party has not publicly identified the ombudsperson in an effort to keep the reporting process impartial and confidential. The NBC Bay Area Investigative Unit contacted the ombudsperson via email for comment but did not receive a response. Investigation Feb 19, 2025 San Francisco Oct 1 The chair of San Francisco’s Democratic Party, Nancy Tung, has faced growing criticism over the system’s failures, with some calling on her to resign, including San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan and the San Francisco Women’s Political Committee – a prominent Women’s political organization. It was under Tung’s leadership that the party created its ambitious new system to investigate sexual misconduct allegations in politics. However, by Tung’s own admission, the process broke down even before the first complaint could be reviewed. “The first time out of the gate, we did not do right by Brad Chapin,” Tung said during a Democratic Party meeting last month. “We did not do right by survivors.” Tung declined to speak with NBC Bay Area on camera but has denied political interference played any role in the delay. Nancy Tung, chair of the San Francisco Democratic Party, has publicly apologized for the failures involved in executing the party’s first-ever sexual misconduct reporting system. In e-mail messages to NBC Bay Area, Tung explained that the problem came down to a basic failure in how the system was set up. According to Tung, the ombudsperson was the only person with access to online complaints, with no backup system to notify anyone else once a new complaint arrived. “The Ombuds was not given explicit instructions on when or with what frequency to check the email,” Tung wrote. Tung told NBC Bay Area the party has since addressed the problem and expects future complaints to be handled in a “timely manner.” At a recent San Francisco Democratic Party meeting, Tung also disclosed that the ombudsperson resigned, citing personal reasons, leaving the party searching for a replacement. For Chapin, the party’s nearly four-month delay in responding to his allegations was only the beginning of his disappointment with the reporting program. The SF DCCC’s complaint review process ended without determining whether the alleged assault occurred. Instead, the party concluded the allegations fell outside the scope of its misconduct policy because the alleged assault neither occurred at an official Democratic Party event nor arose in the context of political activity. “The event in question is not claimed to have occurred at an official meeting or at any sponsored event of the SFDCCC or any chartered club, and was not in the context of any official or unofficial communication or interaction in the context of conducting any political activity,” the party’s judicial commission wrote in August. “This is not a determination on the merits of whether a sexual assault occurred.” That finding left Chapin questioning why the party accepted his complaint for review in the first place. Chapin said he made it clear to investigators from the very beginning that the alleged sexual assault did not occur at a Democratic Party event. Chapin shared his frustration in August when he addressed the Democratic County Central Committee publicly at one of its regular meetings. “When I went to your attorneys, I asked them explicitly if this was a waste of my time, because none of this happened at a Democratic Party event and you knew that,” Chapin said tearfully. “This is a sham.” On the very same day the party informed Chapin his allegations fell outside the scope of its misconduct policy, the San Francisco Democratic Party voted to endorse the man Chapin accused of sexual assault, Manny Yekutiel, in his campaign for San Francisco’s District 8 Supervisor seat. “There was harm caused,” said Ruth Ferguson, who was one of the volunteers the party consulted to develop the new sexual misconduct reporting program. “It was really bad.” Ferguson, who was recently elected to serve on the City College of San Francisco Board of Trustees, was part of the initial planning process for the sexual misconduct reporting system but was not involved in implementing the program. Speaking to NBC Bay Area, she criticized how the accountability system handled its very first complaint. “I think that in Brad’s case, the process failed,” she told NBC Bay Area. “I think it’s really important for us to always have the courage to reevaluate and to understand that we’re not going to get things right all the time.” Ruth Ferguson, who has been public about her past experiences suffering sexual harassment within politics, helped design a new sexual misconduct reporting program for the San Francisco Democratic Party. Ferguson understands the stakes. Last year, in an interview with NBC Bay Area, she spoke about her desire to be involved in the planning process, in part, because of her own experience of suffering sexual harassment in politics. The incident, she said, occurred in 2019 at the hands of a male supervisor while she worked as a legislative staffer for a California state lawmaker. “There was a point where I thought my life was over,” Ferguson tearfully told NBC Bay Area last year. “I felt like all that I was and had worked toward and the whole core of who I was, was just like decimated.” Ferguson says the party’s decision to dismiss the allegations as outside its jurisdiction runs counter to discussions she recalls during the system’s development about whether misconduct outside official party events should also be investigated. “We talked about that quite a bit,” she said. “We need to clean up the language and the policy so that it is explicit whether or not the DCCC has jurisdiction over incidents that occur not at Democratic Party events.” Less than two months after the party endorsed Yekutiel, it withdrew its endorsement after new allegations surfaced from two other men accusing Yekutiel of sexual assault. Since then, Chapin said he has received apologies from several San Francisco political leaders, including Nancy Tung. He says he is not interested in publicly shaming those responsible for the broken reporting process but instead wants to help create a better system that doesn’t fail someone else. “There has to be a system to hold people accountable and prevent people with power from abusing other people,” Chapin said. “I’m hopeful because I have to be and because I’m going do everything in my power to make sure that happens.” Contact The Investigative Unit submit tips | 1-888-996-TIPS | e-mail Bigad Follow @BigadShaban on social media Bigad Shaban

headlines.description: An ambitious and self-described “first-of-its-kind system” designed to hold San Francisco politicians accountable for sexual misconduct failed its very first test, leaving a sexual assault complaint unanswered for nearly four months. The NBC Bay Area Investigative Unit uncovered a basic oversight that party leaders say contributed to the failure: the person responsible for reviewing complaints was never told how often to check the inbox. The new reporting system was supposed to fill a gap in political accountability. As NBC Bay Area reported last year, political campaigns – unlike traditional workplaces – often lack formal procedures for reporting and investigating sexual misconduct. San Francisco’s Democratic Party had also been marred by sexual misconduct allegations against several prominent figures in local Democratic politics. In response, the San Francisco Democratic County Central Committee, or DCCC, recruited volunteers from across the country, consulted survivors of sexual abuse, and enlisted pro bono attorneys to research allegations and build a reporting process independent of party leadership. When the first complaint arrived, however, the system failed at its most basic task – ensuring someone responded. “At best, they were neglecting their responsibilities,” said Brad Chapin, a San Francisco-based political organizer who submitted the complaint. “At worst, it was intentional to protect and provide cover for Manny.” Manny Yekutiel, once considered a leading candidate for a seat on San Francisco’s Board of Supervisors, is the politician Chapin accused of sexual assault. Yekutiel did not respond to NBC Bay Area’s request for comment but has publicly denied the allegations. After two other men accused him of sexual misconduct on Oct. 1, Yekutiel dropped out of the race, but continued to deny assaulting anyone. At a house party in 2020, Chapin says Yekutiel cornered him and stuck his hand down Chapin’s pants. “I think I was just sort of shocked,” Chapin said. “Like, what is happening?” In a police report Chapin filed in April, he said Yekutiel grabbed his testicles in an “aggressive manner…like an animal.” “I tried to get away,” Chapin said during an interview with the NBC Bay Area Investigative Unit. “I was like begging him to let me go and he would squeeze harder and pull me back.” Yekutiel has not been charged with a crime, but the San Francisco Police Department told NBC Bay Area the “case remains open.” Text messages Chapin provided to NBC Bay Area show he told a friend about the alleged assault shortly after it happened, but for years Chapin didn’t formally report the incident to law enforcement or officials at the San Francisco Democratic Party. That changed when Chapin learned of Yekutiel’s campaign for San Francisco’s District 8 Supervisor seat, which includes the Castro, Noe Valley, and parts of the Mission District. Chapin worried that, if elected, Yekutiel could use his position of power to harm others, a fear Chapin said was rooted in what he described as Yekutiel’s brazen behavior during the alleged assault. “If he was willing to do that, in that way, within just seconds of seeing me … there’s no way he only did it to me,” Chapin said. “I kind of had the sense that it would be really hard for most people to come forward.” Brad Chapin formally submitted a complaint through the San Francisco Democratic Party’s sexual misconduct reporting system, alleging he was sexually assaulted in 2020 by Manny Yekutiel, a well-known bookstore owner and, at one point, a leading political candidate in the race for District 8 Supervisor in San Francisco. Documents Chapin provided to NBC Bay Area show that he submitted an official complaint to San Francisco’s Democratic Party on March 3, detailing the alleged assault. After more than a month of silence, Chapin submitted his complaint a second time on April 16. A week later, he also reported the assault to the San Francisco Police Department. While police detectives followed up with Chapin as part of their investigation, two more months went by with Chapin still not receiving any response from the judicial arm of San Francisco’s Democratic Party. Chapin then went to the press with his allegations. On June 30, the San Francisco Standard published a story on Chapin’s allegations. Within hours of that story’s publication, San Francisco’s Democratic Party finally responded. The ombudsperson, responsible for receiving complaints under the party’s new reporting system, e-mailed Chapin saying his “complaint has been received and is currently under review.” That message came nearly four months after he initially reported the sexual assault to the San Francisco Democratic Party. “That’s when I heard back from them,” Chapin recalled. “It was hard not to feel that it was to provide cover for Manny.” The Democratic Party has not publicly identified the ombudsperson in an effort to keep the reporting process impartial and confidential. The NBC Bay Area Investigative Unit contacted the ombudsperson via email for comment but did not receive a response. Investigation Feb 19, 2025 San Francisco Oct 1 The chair of San Francisco’s Democratic Party, Nancy Tung, has faced growing criticism over the system’s failures, with some calling on her to resign, including San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan and the San Francisco Women’s Political Committee – a prominent Women’s political organization. It was under Tung’s leadership that the party created its ambitious new system to investigate sexual misconduct allegations in politics. However, by Tung’s own admission, the process broke down even before the first complaint could be reviewed. “The first time out of the gate, we did not do right by Brad Chapin,” Tung said during a Democratic Party meeting last month. “We did not do right by survivors.” Tung declined to speak with NBC Bay Area on camera but has denied political interference played any role in the delay. Nancy Tung, chair of the San Francisco Democratic Party, has publicly apologized for the failures involved in executing the party’s first-ever sexual misconduct reporting system. In e-mail messages to NBC Bay Area, Tung explained that the problem came down to a basic failure in how the system was set up. According to Tung, the ombudsperson was the only person with access to online complaints, with no backup system to notify anyone else once a new complaint arrived. “The Ombuds was not given explicit instructions on when or with what frequency to check the email,” Tung wrote. Tung told NBC Bay Area the party has since addressed the problem and expects future complaints to be handled in a “timely manner.” At a recent San Francisco Democratic Party meeting, Tung also disclosed that the ombudsperson resigned, citing personal reasons, leaving the party searching for a replacement. For Chapin, the party’s nearly four-month delay in responding to his allegations was only the beginning of his disappointment with the reporting program. The SF DCCC’s complaint review process ended without determining whether the alleged assault occurred. Instead, the party concluded the allegations fell outside the scope of its misconduct policy because the alleged assault neither occurred at an official Democratic Party event nor arose in the context of political activity. “The event in question is not claimed to have occurred at an official meeting or at any sponsored event of the SFDCCC or any chartered club, and was not in the context of any official or unofficial communication or interaction in the context of conducting any political activity,” the party’s judicial commission wrote in August. “This is not a determination on the merits of whether a sexual assault occurred.” That finding left Chapin questioning why the party accepted his complaint for review in the first place. Chapin said he made it clear to investigators from the very beginning that the alleged sexual assault did not occur at a Democratic Party event. Chapin shared his frustration in August when he addressed the Democratic County Central Committee publicly at one of its regular meetings. “When I went to your attorneys, I asked them explicitly if this was a waste of my time, because none of this happened at a Democratic Party event and you knew that,” Chapin said tearfully. “This is a sham.” On the very same day the party informed Chapin his allegations fell outside the scope of its misconduct policy, the San Francisco Democratic Party voted to endorse the man Chapin accused of sexual assault, Manny Yekutiel, in his campaign for San Francisco’s District 8 Supervisor seat. “There was harm caused,” said Ruth Ferguson, who was one of the volunteers the party consulted to develop the new sexual misconduct reporting program. “It was really bad.” Ferguson, who was recently elected to serve on the City College of San Francisco Board of Trustees, was part of the initial planning process for the sexual misconduct reporting system but was not involved in implementing the program. Speaking to NBC Bay Area, she criticized how the accountability system handled its very first complaint. “I think that in Brad’s case, the process failed,” she told NBC Bay Area. “I think it’s really important for us to always have the courage to reevaluate and to understand that we’re not going to get things right all the time.” Ruth Ferguson, who has been public about her past experiences suffering sexual harassment within politics, helped design a new sexual misconduct reporting program for the San Francisco Democratic Party. Ferguson understands the stakes. Last year, in an interview with NBC Bay Area, she spoke about her desire to be involved in the planning process, in part, because of her own experience of suffering sexual harassment in politics. The incident, she said, occurred in 2019 at the hands of a male supervisor while she worked as a legislative staffer for a California state lawmaker. “There was a point where I thought my life was over,” Ferguson tearfully told NBC Bay Area last year. “I felt like all that I was and had worked toward and the whole core of who I was, was just like decimated.” Ferguson says the party’s decision to dismiss the allegations as outside its jurisdiction runs counter to discussions she recalls during the system’s development about whether misconduct outside official party events should also be investigated. “We talked about that quite a bit,” she said. “We need to clean up the language and the policy so that it is explicit whether or not the DCCC has jurisdiction over incidents that occur not at Democratic Party events.” Less than two months after the party endorsed Yekutiel, it withdrew its endorsement after new allegations surfaced from two other men accusing Yekutiel of sexual assault. Since then, Chapin said he has received apologies from several San Francisco political leaders, including Nancy Tung. He says he is not interested in publicly shaming those responsible for the broken reporting process but instead wants to help create a better system that doesn’t fail someone else. “There has to be a system to hold people accountable and prevent people with power from abusing other people,” Chapin said. “I’m hopeful because I have to be and because I’m going do everything in my power to make sure that happens.” Contact The Investigative Unit submit tips | 1-888-996-TIPS | e-mail Bigad Follow @BigadShaban on social media Bigad Shaban
